findings.passage: The Six evidence also clusters in real danger (a police raid, frontier AI risk, a Vatican stage) and in professional speech, where fear is reasonable on its face. The Four evidence comes from his private life, across years, in his own words.
findings.problem: This is the load-bearing step of the Four-over-Six argument, and the record contradicts it. The strongest Six material is also private and first-person. The same 2022 dating doc (S04, opened 2026-11-05) lists under 'Cons': 'I have mild issues with anxiety. I often irrationally worry that people don't like me. In relationships, I worry a lot about not being good enough and my partner leaving me. I also find it hard to be spontaneous'. Under 'Why past relationships didn't work out' it says 'Partner was poly, I was anxiously attached' and 'My partner valued spontaneity and adventure, but I found this anxiety producing (especially when adventure involved things that were mildly dangerous)'. The 2020 essay's 'alone forever' worry (C55) is private too. The draft quotes some of this in the Six section and then claims the Six evidence is situational and professional, and it never mentions the anxious-attachment and risk-aversion lines. The doc's past-incompatibilities section ('in case they can help us avoid similar incompatibilities') is a screening and contingency move inside the very document the draft reads as pure 'being seen'.
findings.acceptance_test: The clustering sentence is removed or rewritten so it does not claim the Six evidence is mostly situational or professional. The Six case acknowledges, with attribution, that his private self-description includes anxious attachment and anxiety about mildly dangerous adventure (S04). The Four-over-Six argument then rests on a discriminator that survives this evidence. For example: the content of his private fears (not being good enough, not being liked) is shame-coded and points to the heart triad more than to security as such. That reasoning is stated as inference, not fact.

findings.passage: Sad, across contexts and years, even about state misconduct. Rarely angry, rarely suspicious.
findings.problem: The word-count argument is selective, and it carries temperament weight in the type answer ('sadness more often than panic'), the body, and the Why-not-6 FAQ ('his habitual word for disappointment is "sad," not alarmed'). In the August 2021 interpretability interview (S02), Olah himself says 'worried'/'worry'/'nervous'/'nervousness' about 15 times and 'sad' about 3 times. Some of these are personal, not risk analysis: 'I feel really nervous to describe these as being about concepts', 'I just have this nervousness that when you take a bunch of ideas that aren't mature...', 'I do worry a lot about races'. 'Sad' is his word for losses and disappointments. 'Worried'/'nervous' is his word for threats and for exposing his own claims. Counting only the loss register and calling it his baseline is the stereotype of the melancholy Four, not a discriminator.
findings.acceptance_test: The prose and FAQ either drop the lexical tally as type evidence or report both registers honestly (sad for losses, worried/nervous for threats and for exposing his own ideas, both in his own 2021 words). The 'not alarmed' FAQ wording and the 'sadness more often than panic' framing no longer imply that fear-language is rare in his record.

findings.passage: **He calls himself scrupulous**, which is One and Six territory, though the anger that marks a One is absent from his record.
findings.problem: Type 1 is dismissed on a false premise. The draft's own quotes show anger: 'There was a lot of outrage' and 'I'm really outraged at just the appalling ethics of it' (S01). In context he also says the case 'really deeply soured my views' and that 'where I wind up is something like, just being really disappointed'. Line 185 then misreads his two-hats answer as 'Setting the outrage aside as one hat and landing on sadness'. He holds both hats at once and sets neither aside. The 'Rarely angry' line repeats the error. Meanwhile the One case is stronger than one sentence allows: 'moral loneliness' is about moral conviction, he writes 'I'm very dedicated to doing what I believe to be morally right', friends compare dating him to dating 'a moral philosopher' (S04), he went vegetarian at four on moral grounds, and he writes principles essays (S18). The only test separating 4 from 1 is the anger claim, and the record refutes it.
findings.acceptance_test: No sentence claims anger is absent from his record, and the two-hats answer is described as holding outrage and sadness together. The One alternative gets a real discriminator in a sentence or two. For example: his moral loneliness is narrated as being alone in feeling and wanting companions who feel the same ('part of me opens up. I am more myself'), not as correcting others to a standard. He also explicitly does not want a partner who shares his beliefs ('the last thing I'd want would be for either of us to feel constrained in our independent moral judgment'). The line is labeled as inference.

findings.passage: And the shape is the courtroom again. Frightened, then present, then saying the uncomfortable thing out loud. Take the Vatican out of his story and the argument above still stands.
findings.problem: The draft calls a teenager who is afraid and goes to court anyway 'a textbook counterphobic Six'. Here it shows the same fear, then approach, then speaking up, recurring 16 years later. Then it sets the pattern aside without rebutting it. A pattern that repeats across 2010 and 2026 is evidence for the counterphobic reading, not a reason to discount the Vatican. Removing the Vatican does not remove the 2010 instance, which the draft concedes is textbook Six. The Why-not-6 section answers the phobic Six (reassurance, doubt) and uses optimism against it. It never answers the counterphobic subtype it raised itself, and counterphobic Sixes also defy authority and voice optimism. The record holds a usable discriminator the draft leaves implicit. In 2010 his fear was partly for his own group ('I was scared for myself and for all of my friends that maybe they were going to now come after all of us'), which is Six-coded. But his repeated stated reason is identification with the abandoned ('support people when others don't'), not testing or defending against the threat.
findings.acceptance_test: The Why-not-6 section addresses the counterphobic Six reading directly and names what separates it from Four in this record, with sources and inference limits. The section quotes the group-fear half of the 2010 answer instead of omitting it. The Vatican paragraph no longer implies that the recurring fear-then-approach shape is neutral or Four-favoring.

findings.passage: He owns the envy, through the pastor, of people who have what he lacks.
findings.problem: Envy is the Four's defining passion, so this sentence carries type weight, but it states an inference as fact. The source (S08, opened via Thread Reader) says Ames 'grapples with jealousy and resentment towards a character who has a child by accident and is a terrible father, while Ames is childless and alone. That's something that's come to resonate with me more over that time.' The referent of 'That' could be the jealousy or the childless solitude. The June 2021 thread corrects the comparison ('I shouldn't compare'). He also gives a protective reason for the sacred framing: 'I also suspect it might protect against some of the ways loneliness can be corrosive'. That is coping language the Six and Five readings could also claim.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence says that the pastor's jealousy is something he says has 'come to resonate' with him. It labels the envy reading as an interpretation ('this suggests'), and it does not present envy as something he openly owns.

findings.passage: A Five would be satisfied to understand it. Olah wants you to love it, or to grieve it, with him.
findings.problem: The Five is dismissed with a stereotype, and the support is one reporter's 'as if' impression (S13). A researcher who co-founded a journal for explanation (Distill) and wants readers to see what he sees fits an expressive Five as easily. Later the draft absorbs the Five evidence (memorized neurons, micromarriages) with 'A 5 wing would fit'. That is the wing-as-escape-hatch the standard warns against: the Five counterevidence first loses on a caricature and is then reclaimed as a wing.
findings.acceptance_test: The Five contrast rests on a sourced behavioral difference, such as his repeated public disclosure of longing and his stated need for 'moral connection' versus a Five's guarding of resources and privacy. It does not rest on what a Five 'would be satisfied' with. The wing line is either removed or framed as optional and uncertain ('if a wing is visible at all'), not as the explanation for the counterevidence.

findings.passage: His word for disappointment, across a decade of interviews, is "sad."
findings.problem: The evidence record (C25) dates the 'sad' instances from 2021 to 2026, five years, not a decade. Overstating the span inflates the stability of the type marker. Similarly, 'moral loneliness' appears once in the opened record (S04, 2022), so 'he reaches for a phrase of his own' implies a habit the sources do not show.
findings.acceptance_test: The span matches the cited record (2021–2026), and 'reaches for' is replaced by wording that reflects a single documented use, or a second dated use is cited.

protected_passages.passage: Fear came first. Then he walked toward the thing that scared him.
protected_passages.reason: An honest hook that opens with the strongest datum against the article's own type. It sets up a real typing contest instead of a foregone conclusion.

protected_passages.passage: What would change this read is named colleagues saying that, under stress at work, he habitually seeks reassurance, defers to authority or expects the worst. The research for this page found no such account.
protected_passages.reason: A concrete, falsifiable discriminator stated in reader language. This is exactly what the standard asks for and rarely gets.

protected_passages.passage: The bullying isn't offered here as the cause of his type; the sources describe the experience, not what it did to him.
protected_passages.reason: Explicitly refuses an invented childhood wound, which is the most common typing overreach.

protected_passages.passage: None of these overturns the read. Together they describe a Four who is gentler, more orderly and more optimistic than the type's reputation, and who meets his own sadness with a statistics joke as often as a poem.
protected_passages.reason: Lets counterevidence change the portrait instead of explaining it away, and the micromarriages detail makes it specific to Olah.

protected_passages.passage: He put the core of it best himself, writing about *Gilead*: "When I can inhabit this mindset of loneliness being sacred in some sense, it adds a kind of beauty to an otherwise quite sad experience."
protected_passages.reason: A verified, context-faithful quote (S08) that ties the aesthetic motive to the emotional one in his own words. This is the best single piece of Four evidence.

assessment: Type 4 is defensible at the evidence record's stated medium confidence. The chosen discriminator is the right kind of test: when something he wants is missing, does he move toward security or toward meaning and being seen? The shame-coded content of his private fears (not good enough, not liked), the Gilead thread and the 'support people when others don't' motive give it real support. But the draft applies the test selectively. It claims the Six evidence is situational or professional, when the most personal document also contains anxious attachment and anxiety about mildly dangerous adventure (S04). It leans on a 'sad' word tally while 'worried'/'nervous' dominate his own 2021 interview (S02). It dismisses Type 1 on an absent-anger premise that its own quotes refute. And it raises the counterphobic Six, shows the pattern recurring in 2010 and 2026, then never rebuts it. None of these alone flips the type, but together they mean the Four case currently wins by framing in places where it should win by discriminator. contested_typing stays true; the alternative is seriously engaged. Similarity advisory: the tripped matches (mike-faist, hunter-schafer) are the shared phrase 'whose core emotion is shame' plus head-type/fear vocabulary. That is ordinary type vocabulary required by house voice, not reuse of an argument, and the Olah-specific argument is not formulaic. Wings and arrows are mostly kept out of the argument, except the convenient 5-wing line. I re-opened S01, S02, S03, S04 and S08 for this review; S13 (NYT via SLTrib) was not re-opened.
